title: Calissons de Provence
subtitle: Provençal almond and candied peel confections with royal icing
excerpt: Calissons are diamond-shaped confections from Aix-en-Provence made from ground almonds blended with candied fruit, shaped, then glazed with a thin layer of royal icing. The texture inside is dense, smooth, and marzipan-like with a pronounced almond flavour and a hint of orange blossom. They are one of the thirteen traditional Provençal Christmas desserts and are made in large batches that keep for weeks in a tin.
sourceNotes: Calissons de Provence are documented in French food history from at least the 15th century; the town of Aix-en-Provence has had a Confrérie du Calisson since 1998 and the confection has protected geographical indication (IGP) status in France since 2020. Traditionally the paste is made from Provence almonds and confited melon. The technique follows standard Provençal confectionery practice as documented in French regional cookery references including Jean-Noël Escudier's La Véritable Cuisine Provençale et Niçoise (1953).

recipe.batchNotes: Scales directly. Make in double or triple batches; they keep well.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Layer in an airtight tin between sheets of baking paper. Keep at cool room temperature for up to 3 weeks.

content.text: Calissons are made in two stages: first blending ground almonds with candied peel and orange blossom water into a smooth, firm paste, then glazing the cut shapes with a thin, flat-white royal icing that sets hard. The paste must be firm enough to roll and cut cleanly; the icing must set to a matte, just-opaque finish rather than a thick white coat. Getting the balance of these two textures right is what distinguishes a calisson from a marzipan sweet.

Blitz the {{mixed-peel}} in a food processor until it forms a coarse paste, about 1 minute. Add {{ground-almonds}} and {{icing-sugar}} and pulse until combined. Add {{orange-blossom-water}} one tablespoon at a time, pulsing between additions, until the mixture comes together into a firm, smooth paste that holds a ball when pressed. It should not be sticky. If it is too dry to come together, add a few more drops of orange blossom water.

Tip the paste onto a sheet of baking paper and roll to 8 mm thickness. Cover with a second sheet of paper and leave to rest at room temperature for 1 hour. Resting firms the paste slightly and makes it easier to cut cleanly.

Use a small oval or diamond cutter (a traditional calisson cutter is about 5 cm long) to cut shapes from the paste, pressing firmly and lifting straight up. Transfer to a wire rack set over a clean baking tray. Re-roll the trimmings and cut again.
Make and apply the icing glaze

Whisk {{egg-whites}} with {{icing-sugar}} and {{lemon-juice}} until smooth, thick, and pourable but not stiff. The consistency should coat the back of a spoon and hold a ribbon for 2 seconds before dissolving. Spoon a small amount onto each calisson and spread to the edges with the back of the spoon. The layer should be thin, just enough to form an opaque white coat. Leave at room temperature for 1 to 2 hours until the icing has set completely and is no longer tacky.
